method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

items.assessment: Severe worsening pain with fever differs from expected gas; analgesic/antipyretic relief cannot substitute for urgent complication assessment. Key is concise and alternatives now reflect real symptom-normalization errors.
Throat-anaesthetic recovery and swallow safety govern intake. Thirst, absent abdominal pain and fixed time alone are inadequate readiness criteria.
Flank pain plus tachycardia and falling pressure after biopsy requires bleeding assessment/escalation. Dry dressing and sedation attribution are plausible but unsafe normalization errors.
New anticoagulant disclosure requires procedural-team review before elective biopsy; normal haemoglobin and chart update alone do not resolve risk planning.
Painful inability to void after cystoscopy warrants prompt assessment; expected burning advice, fluids alone and culture-first sequencing miss retention.
Persistent severe pain/vomiting after ERCP requires complication review; a normal procedure report and temporary nausea relief do not establish recovery.

proposedChanges.stem: A client returning from liver biopsy looks pale and reports new lightheadedness. Which assessments most directly evaluate possible bleeding with impaired perfusion? Select all that apply.
options: The client’s usual response to venepuncture
Vital signs and their change from baseline
Abdominal discomfort and evidence of bleeding
The planned timing of the next oral analgesic
why: A usual fainting response may add history but does not establish the cause of this post-biopsy change.
Vital-sign trends help identify circulatory deterioration.
Abdominal findings and bleeding evidence help assess a procedural complication.
Medication timing does not directly evaluate circulation or bleeding.

items.assessment: Current acute renal decline must reach the imaging team; old results and unilateral hydration do not establish current contrast risk. The correct action communicates rather than universally cancels imaging.
Early coordinated support addresses severe claustrophobia before an elective MRI. Unverified sedative/transport planning is a realistic incomplete preparation alternative.
Current possibility of pregnancy triggers screening/team communication; an old result, brief exposure or universal deferral are inadequate substitutes for individualized imaging decisions.
Conflicting orders require responsible-team clarification before intake. Newest-order assumption, universal fasting and colleague habit do not resolve the specific conflict.
Accessible agreed cues before biopsy preserve timely communication. Increased volume, post-sedation teaching and aid removal without substitute can fail the case-specific need.
Safety content is now complete, but the key is conspicuously longer and more comprehensive than alternatives. Shorten it while retaining urgent responsiveness/ventilation assessment.

options: Discharge if a relative promises close observation
Allow additional sleep and reassess at the next routine recovery check
Use the elapsed recovery time because the procedure was uncomplicated
Assess responsiveness and breathing and obtain urgent recovery review
why: Home supervision does not replace adequate immediate recovery.
Difficulty arousing needs active immediate assessment, not a routine deferred check.
Elapsed time does not establish physiological readiness.
Assess airway protection, ventilation and responsiveness promptly while obtaining appropriate help.

items.assessment: Progressive bright-red bleeding plus dyspnoea changes urgency compared with an isolated streak or improving local irritation. Options are now comparable post-bronchoscopy observations.
Posture-dependent headache after lumbar puncture is a specific useful pattern to report. Supine score alone, presumed dehydration and unsupported migraine attribution miss that context.

New unilateral pleuritic pain, reduced breath sounds and dyspnoea after thoracentesis require urgent assessment. Imaging should accompany, not precede recognition/escalation of respiratory compromise.

Accessible written warnings plus an agreed support person and action-plan check address post-sedation recall. Signatures and repeated verbal delivery do not demonstrate understanding. Key is somewhat longer but its clinically distinct support/verification approach is necessary, not merely generic comprehensiveness.
The SATA wrong options remain deliberately incomplete reports with only/without qualifiers. Make all options parallel information and ask for immediate recovery monitoring needs.

proposedChanges.stem: When receiving a client after an invasive procedure, which handover details most directly guide immediate recovery monitoring? Select all that apply.
options: The originally planned date of discharge
The client’s usual exercise routine before admission
Sedation given and the last observations
why: The original discharge plan does not establish present recovery needs.
Baseline activity can inform later planning but does not specify immediate postprocedure monitoring.
These guide current restrictions and required observations.
Sedative exposure and recent observations help anticipate and detect recovery complications.
